growth_story.headline: Oil lifted Syria in the 1990s and faded after; war from 2011 more than halved income per person, and a recovery since 2025 is not yet in the data.
growth_story.arc: Income per person grew 4.3 percent a year in 1990–1998, when new oil fields lifted output, exports and state revenue. Oil production turned down after 1995, and growth slowed to 0.7 percent a year in 1999–2006 even as the government slowly opened a state-run economy. Income per person peaked in 2011, the year the uprising began and turned into civil war; it then fell 26.0 percent in 2012 and 22.6 percent in 2013, so the 2007–2014 era averaged -5.5 percent a year as fighting destroyed capital, cut oil output and split the country. The fall slowed but did not stop in 2015–2022, at -2.1 percent a year, and by 2022 income per person was 53.5 percent below its 2011 peak, about where it first was in 1972. The data end in 2022, while the IMF and World Bank describe a recovery under way since 2025 as sanctions were lifted and refugees came home.

threads.title: The rise and fall of oil
threads.text: Oil fields found from the 1970s to the 1990s lifted output, exports and state revenue, and income per person grew 4.3 percent a year in 1990–1998. Production then turned down after 1995 while home use of energy kept rising, and by the late 2000s Syria again bought more oil than it sold.

since_last_year.text: Over the past year the IMF and World Bank have gone from describing early signs of recovery to a quickening one. The World Bank's October 2026 outlook says activity strengthened in the first half of 2026 on rebuilding, better transport links, and higher farm and oil output, and that most remaining restrictions were eased. It also says the Middle East conflict raised energy costs and brought inflation back.

growth_story.tension: In 2009 the IMF called Syria's economic performance strong, with robust growth outside oil, yet income per person rose only 0.7 percent a year in 1999–2006 and fell in 2007: falling oil output held down overall growth, and the population grew fast, swelled by refugees from Iraq. Today the sources describe a recovery that is speeding up, but the data stop in 2022, when income per person was still falling (-3.9 percent), and the millions of returning Syrians raise the population that any new output is shared among.
